title: The Interview Framework
summary: The standard shape of a 45-minute system design interview — requirements, estimation, high-level design, deep dive, wrap-up — and how to move through it without sounding scripted.

slides.markdown:
A system design interview isn't a free-form conversation — it has a predictable shape: **clarify requirements**, **estimate scale**, **sketch a high-level design**, **go deep on 1-2 components**, and **wrap up**. Interviewers expect you to move through these phases, not wander.

Think of it like a structured tour, not an open hike: the framework tells you which room to walk into next, but you still choose what to say in each room. This topic covers the shape itself, how to hold it loosely, and the mistakes that come from ignoring it.

slides.sectionTitle: The standard 45-minute shape: requirements, estimation, HLD, deep dive, wrap-up
slides.markdown:
Most system design interviews — from a 10-person startup to a FAANG onsite — follow roughly the same five phases: **requirements** (5-10 min), **capacity estimation** (5 min), **high-level design** (10-15 min), **deep dive** (15-20 min), and **wrap-up** (2-5 min).

The phases build on each other: your estimation numbers decide which components need to be distributed, your high-level design decides what's worth a deep dive, and the deep dive is what actually gets scored hardest. Skipping a phase doesn't save time — it just means the interviewer has to drag you back to it later.

Treat the shape as a checklist you carry in your head, not a script you read aloud.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the framework as a timeline with minutes allocated
slides.markdown:
![45-minute interview timeline with five segments, Deep Dive largest](assets/interview-timeline.svg)

The timeline isn't evenly split: **deep dive gets the most time and the most scoring weight**, because it's where you show judgment under detail, not just recall.

If you're at minute 20 and still sketching the high-level design, that's a signal to compress it — not a reason to ask the interviewer for extra time.

slides.sectionTitle: Why skipping requirements is the most common failure mode
slides.markdown:
The single most common way candidates lose points in the first ten minutes is jumping straight to a design before requirements are pinned down. It feels efficient — you recognize the problem, so why ask questions? — but it produces a design that answers the wrong problem.

For example, sketching a database schema and hash function for "design a URL shortener" without asking about the read:write ratio or custom-alias support risks over-engineering for writes when the real workload is 100:1 read-heavy.

The fix costs almost nothing: two minutes of questions before drawing a single box. Interviewers read that discipline as senior signal, independent of the design itself.

slides.sectionTitle: How much time to spend on each phase, and adjusting on the fly
slides.markdown:
The 5/5/15/20/5-minute split is a **default, not a contract**. Adjust it live based on two signals: how the interviewer reacts, and how much ground the problem actually needs covered.

If the interviewer keeps nodding and glancing at the clock during requirements, that's a cue to wrap up early. If a design has an unusually large estimation surface — a system with wildly different read and write scale, like a social feed — spend an extra two minutes there since it changes every downstream decision.

The skill being tested isn't clock-watching, it's **noticing when a phase has done its job** and moving on before it overstays.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a rigid framework vs a natural conversation
slides.markdown:
Using the framework word-for-word every time reads as memorized, not skilled. The difference is in how you carry it, not what you cover.

| | Rigid framework | Natural conversation |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | "First I'll gather requirements, then estimate..." | Just starts asking good questions |
| Transitions | Announces each phase by name | Moves naturally: "Given that traffic, let's sketch..." |
| Feels like | A recital | A senior engineer thinking out loud |
| Risk | Sounds scripted, brittle under a curveball | Same coverage, no scripted feel |

**How to decide:** keep the phases as a private checklist, but let the interviewer's questions and reactions decide the pacing and the words — never narrate the framework itself out loud.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: jumping straight to a detailed architecture before requirements are clear
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I recognize this problem, so I can start drawing the architecture immediately — it'll show I'm confident."

**Why it's wrong:** without functional and non-functional requirements pinned down, an interviewer can't tell if your design is thoughtful or just a memorized template. Worse, half the natural follow-up questions become moot because they were about scale or features you never asked about.

**Correct model:** confidence shows up in how well the design fits the stated requirements, not in how fast you started drawing. Spend the first few minutes asking, even when you're sure you know the answer — it's rarely wasted, and it's never read as weakness.
